scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In 1116, Emperor Huizong gifted 428 instruments and 572 costumes to Korea, effectively creating a time capsule of ancient Chinese melodies that were later lost in their homeland.
This is Yayue. 11th century BCE to present.
on_screen: Title card: Yayue · China · 11th century BCE to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Established in the Western Zhou dynasty, yayue was commissioned by the Duke of Zhou.
It incorporated shamanistic traditions and early folk music.
It remained central to imperial ceremonies until the end of the Qing dynasty, with major developments occurring during the Song dynasty.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Yayue was performed for ceremonies honoring Heaven, Earth, ancestors, and gods.
It was also used for diplomatic meetings, archery contests, hunting expeditions, and celebrations following military victories.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dances are strictly categorized as civil or military.
Civil dancers hold a yue flute in the left hand and a feather plume in the right.
Military dancers hold a shield in the left hand and a battleaxe in the right.
on_screen: Formation: Strict row-based formation (e.g., 8x8, 6x6, 4x4, 2x2) based on social rank.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is monophonic, slow, and stately, with 4-8 beats per phrase.

Instruments are classified into eight material categories: silk (guqin, se), bamboo (dizi, xiao, paixiao, chi), wood (zhu, yu), stone (bianqing), metal (bianzhong, fangxiang), clay (xun), gourd (sheng, yu), and hide (gu).
Listen for the guqin, dizi, xiao, paixiao.
Slow, stately, and monophonic music characterized by the resonance of stone chimes, bronze bells, and various wind instruments, organized into distinct terrace and courtyard ensembles.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: monophonic with little rhythmic variety
scenes.music: the music brief's underscore at its own tempo; drop narration under the hook of a verified recording if licensed, else original

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performances occurred on palace terraces or in courtyards.
Musicians and dancers wore formal court attire.
The spatial arrangement followed five directions, with the orchestra split into yin (terrace) and yang (courtyard) ensembles.
on_screen: Image gallery: 4 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Duke of Zhou (founder), Confucius (philosopher who championed yayue), Emperor Huizong of Song (patron who gifted instruments to Korea), Chen Yang (author of the Yueshu).
Gagaku (Japan), Aak (Korea), Nhã nhạc (Vietnam).
Directly linked to the Six Great Dances of the Zhou dynasty; influenced the development of Confucian ritual music across East Asia.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Yayue is variant of Aak: Korean court music that preserves elements of Chinese yayue from the Song dynasty.
Yayue is variant of Gagaku: Japanese court music influenced by the concept of yayue.
Yayue is variant of Nhã nhạc: Vietnamese court music influenced by the yayue tradition.
on_screen: Graph: the connections with their relation labels

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Yayue is intrinsically linked to Confucian rites, ancestor worship, and ceremonies honoring Heaven and Earth; it is considered a formal, moral, and political instrument of the state.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: Discover the ancient ritual music that defined the moral and political order of the Chinese imperial court.

Instruments: guqin, dizi, xiao, paixiao, chi, zhu, bianqing, bianzhong. Vocal style: singing included in terrace ensemble. Form: ceremonial, monophonic. Mood: stately, formal, solemn. It should sound like this: Slow, stately, and monophonic music characterized by the resonance of stone chimes, bronze bells, and various wind instruments, organized into distinct terrace and courtyard ensembles. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.
